Thus Euripides Andr. 465 said ἀμφιμάτορας κόρους [children of different mothers], which the scholiast explains as τοὺς ἐκ διαφόρων μητέρων, ἐξ ἑνὸς δέ πατρός [those from different mothers, but from one father].
ἀμφιμήτορες [those of different mothers]: brothers born from many mothers. Aeschylus in Heraclidae (fr.70).

where the scholiast explains it as the necessity from different cities, that is, war; for the Greeks were from different cities. With which he compares, not very aptly, ἀμφιμάτορας κόρους [children of different mothers] of Euripides Andr. 465, about which see under ἀμφιμήτωρ [of different mother]. Blomfield rightly understands it as necessity surrounding the city, namely when it was besieged by enemies, as Aeschylus said ἀμφιτειχῆ λεών [the people around the walls] Sept. 290, the people besieging the walls.

Ἄμφις [Amphis]: this is not a syncope, but a transformation; for from Ἀμφιάραος [Amphiaraus] comes Ἄμφις [Amphis], as in Aeschylus (fr. 361)
on the origin of whose name see Lobeck. Pathol. Prol. p. 35 and Thes. vol. 1, 2 p. 255.

Thus corrected from the scholia and Etym. Gud. p. 104, 42 for ἀντίστροφον [turned opposite]. The scholiast explains it as τὴν ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων τῶν μερῶν ἑλισσομένην, ὅ ἐστιν ἀμφιέλισσαν [the one that is coiled from both sides, that is, double-coiled].
I bid you to go into the versatile boat.

The correct accent is αμφισωπος [open on all sides] and περιωπός [conspicuous].
ἀμφίσωπον [open on all sides]: conspicuous, opened from all sides. Aeschylus in Glaucus Potnieus (fr. 35).
